item.title: Missing From a Mass Wedding in India: Brides
item.description:
Abhishek Varma could not shake the feeling that something was wrong on his wedding day.

His parents, desperate to marry him off, had found a man in a nearby village in India who described himself as a matchmaker. All they had to do, he told them, was select an orphaned woman from a photo album and pay around $200 to join a mass wedding.

When the day came in late May, Mr. Varma and about 40 other grooms from several villages arrived at 8 a.m. in wedding kurtas and sherwanis, he said. They waited all day for their brides — until they realized they’d been duped.

“They took the bait,” said Preeti Katare, a police officer handling the case, adding that the victims were rural men in their early 20s to 40s. She added that dozens of others had not come forward out of shame.

The case — in which the purported matchmaker and his accomplices now face fraud charges in the central state of Madhya Pradesh — is an extreme example of a wedding scam in a marriage industry that is notoriously prone to it.

Many scammers in India are lured by the huge sums of money flowing to its marriage market, in which families spend years saving up for a daughter’s wedding clothing, jewelry and dowry — the traditional, yet illegal, payment of cash or assets to the groom. Marriage scams are common enough that Indian newspapers run full-page ads with tips on how to avoid them.

But fraudulent mass weddings are rare. Ram Lal Bhagat, a sub inspector with the Madhya Pradesh Police, said it was the first one he had seen in 40 years on the job.

About a dozen of the victims, including Mr. Varma, filed complaints that led to the purported matchmaker’s arrest and detention in the central state of Madhya Pradesh. In late July, the police there said they had charged the man, Dinesh Bairagi, 45, and four accomplices, including his brother, Mukesh Bairagi, 40.

A lawyer for the Bairagis could not be reached for comment. If convicted, they could face a punishment of up to three years in prison and a fine.

The police said that the Bairagis reaped the equivalent of around $4,000 by charging each man 10,000 to 25,000 rupees ($105 to $260), a significant sum for rural families but a bargain price for a wedding. They “saw an opportunity in this problem where it’s hard for a lower- to middle-income groom to find a bride in a village setting,” Ms. Katare said.

For Abhishek Varma’s parents, arranging his marriage to an orphan was a way to end his relationship with another woman, the daughter of a chauffeur.

Because he was the unemployed son of a farmer from a lower caste, he said, his girlfriend’s parents thought he had little to offer her and threatened to harm his family if the couple did not separate.

Mr. Varma said his family pressured him to choose a bride based on photos of women in an orphanage, and that the matchmakers declined to let him meet her before the wedding.

“They said it was not the rule of the orphanage to have the girls meet strange men like that,” he said in a phone interview. “I had slight doubts, but I had no option but to go along with my family. Honor is everything.”

Mr. Varma, who has a computer science degree but works odd jobs, said that some of his fellow grooms were unemployed young men like him, while others were in their 40s and 50s and considered too old for the marriage market.

More than 5 percent of men in India are unemployed, according to the Ministry of Statistics and Program Implementation, a figure that experts say does not account for the country’s sprawling informal sector. A March report by Azim Premji University in Bengaluru found that nearly 40 percent of recent graduates were unemployed.

Indian families occasionally allow their daughters to marry men who come from a higher caste or have a high earning potential, to justify the cost of a wedding and a dowry, said Gaurav Chiplunkar, a business professor at the University of Virginia who has studied rural India’s marriage market. Those women tend to leave their villages, leaving local men behind.

“The marriage market is so skewed that there are just no brides, or the men are older, or they need women to work in the household while the men go to their jobs in the cities,” he said.

Matching a son to an orphaned woman typically indicates that a family is desperate enough to forego a dowry, which would provide a financial buffer for the groom’s family if he were unemployed, Professor Chiplunkar said.

India’s Parliament passed a law banning dowries in 1961, but the payments are still common and can cost hundreds of dollars, the equivalent of years of income for a rural bride’s family, according to Professor Chiplunkar’s research.

To remedy the shortage of brides, state governments offer financial incentives for mass weddings, which are typically shorter and cheaper than traditional ones that last for days. In Uttar Pradesh, for example, the bride receives around $600 in cash and about $250 worth of wedding paraphernalia. The state’s chief minister said in 2024 that around 400,000 women from poor and ethnic minority families had been married through the program.

State-sponsored mass weddings often take place before key elections. In 2022, Prime Minister Narendra Modi took a break from campaigning in his home state of Gujarat to attend a wedding for more than 500 women who had lost their fathers.

But the fraudulent mass wedding in Madhya Pradesh was not connected to a government program or an election. The police said the family behind it used their reputation in the village to gain their victims’ trust.

“In villages, trust works,” Ms. Katare said. “And they trusted this family.”

As the hours ticked by without any sign of their brides, the celebratory mood gave way to anger. The grooms and their families restlessly paced around the temple in Dewas, the small city where the purported matchmaker had told them to gather.

Around 5 p.m., Mr. Varma said there was a collective sigh of relief when a man from the Bairagi family arrived with more men from his village. They thought it meant that other Bairagis would soon arrive with their brides.

Their relief did not last long: The police were called to the temple soon after dark.

Mr. Varma said he later looked into the photos of the women provided by the matchmakers. They were not orphans, he said, but influencers who had millions of followers on Instagram.

As for his former girlfriend, he said, she is happy that his wedding didn’t work out.

item.title: A Chinese Robot Beat Usain Bolt’s 100-Meter Record. Should We Be Impressed?
item.description:
In 2009, Usain Bolt set the men’s 100-meter dash world record of 9.58 seconds at the World Athletics Championships in Berlin. On Saturday, a humanoid robot developed by the Chinese company X-Humanoid beat that record by 0.19 seconds, according to Chinese state media. The robot ended its sprint by slamming full speed into a padded wall, falling down and being carried away by human assistants.

High-profile feats of robotic athleticism have become increasingly common in China, where a humanoid robotics industry has flourished, aided by generous state support and billions in investment. Robots have danced and performed martial arts at the country’s top events.

At the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing over the weekend, they boxed and participated in soccer matches. One played tennis against a human opponent, moving across the court and angling itself to return volleys. Earlier this year, a robot ran a marathon faster than any human in history.

But what do these robotic superhuman feats amount to?

“Most of the sports the humanoids are doing don’t directly translate into utility for many of the mundane tasks people are trying to get humanoids to perform, like being useful around the house,” said Michael Milford, a professor and director of the robotics center at Queensland University of Technology in Australia.

The robots are “capable in very specific and somewhat contrived events,” he said.

Chinese media has also acknowledged the gulf between athleticism and real-world applications in its coverage of the games.

“A factory robot does not need to win a sprint, nor does a service robot need a medal,” read a commentary in Xinhua, the state news agency. “But every gain in speed, stability and precision on the competition floor can bring robots one step closer to becoming genuinely useful beyond it.”

Even without significant and proven real-world applications, these high-profile displays and the attention they have attracted are already paying some dividends. Unitree Robotics — a humanoid robotics company whose videos of robots performing kung fu, kickboxing and back flips have attracted millions of views online, and whose robots featured heavily at the Humanoid Robot Games last year — debuted on the Shanghai stock market last week. Its shares ended their first day of trading up by more than 460 percent.

Alan Fern, a robotics professor at Oregon State University, was part of a research team that set the Guinness World Record for the fastest 100-meter run by a robot on two legs in 2022. That robot ran it in 24.73 seconds. To go from that, in four years, to X-Humanoid’s 9.39 seconds was an “enormous achievement,” he said.

But he noted that robotics companies have become relatively experienced in making robots that can run, jump and do acrobatics in controlled environments. He added that incremental improvements in these sports are mostly related to developing better hardware and refining the controls, rather than any significant technological breakthrough.

The robot at the games in Beijing that could play tennis against a human was more impressive, he said, because that involved interacting with something unpredictable.

Most robots struggle in situations where they need to adapt to changing situations. Yet the tennis robot had to track a fast-moving ball, decide where to move, coordinate its body and time the strike.

The robots are still far from perfect, with accidents abounding at the games. Robots fell down, sparked small fires and crashed into objects, according to videos of the event. The unusual running style of one machine, with its arms up near its face, earned it the nickname “shy robot” on the social media platform Weibo. Many of the racing robots did not seem capable of slowing down on their own and instead stopped by running into a padded barrier.

The vision of humanoid robots eventually being able to do anything a human can do is still far away, Mr. Fern said.

“Outside entertainment and a limited number of tightly constrained industrial settings, these robots do not yet have the general-purpose intelligence and reliability needed to operate in messy real-world environments,” he said.

Mr. Milford said that it could take many years before robots can safely and reliably perform in everyday settings.

He drew a comparison to self-driving cars: Three or four decades ago, a self-driving car could drive across a continent on highways. But only in recent years has the technology become advanced and safe enough for such cars to be deployed widely and largely without incident.

Car racing may be another good analogy, Mr. Fern said. “We still marvel at the engineering achievements in Formula 1, and some of those advances eventually transfer elsewhere, but we do not interpret every faster lap as a revolution in transportation,” he said.

“Similarly, beating Usain Bolt does not mean that the robot has surpassed humans at locomotion in any general sense,” he added.

Mr. Bolt did not respond to a request for comment.

Siyi Zhaocontributed research.

item.title: Man Who Told of a Childhood With Wolves Dies at 80
item.description:
Marcos Rodríguez Pantoja, whose account of growing up in a remote part of Spain, with the companionship of only wolves and other animals, was analyzed in a case study and adapted into literature and film, died this month at 80, according to the authorities in San Cibrao das Viñas, the municipality where he spent his final years.

Mr. Rodríguez’s story came to light in the mid-1970s, about a decade after he had made what he described as an unwilling return to human society. Gabriel Janer Manila, a writer, heard about the case from a friend and wanted to learn more.

“At first, it seemed like a fabrication. It couldn’t be true,” Mr. Janer said in a 2010 interview with the site Anika Entre Libros.

But he came to believe to believe the tale, finding corroboration for Mr. Rodríguez’s claims from witnesses and other research. Mr. Janer would go on to write a study about Mr. Rodríguez’s childhood and, later, a novel called “I Played With Wolves,” originally published in 2009.

The story also inspired a 2010 film directed by Gerardo Oliveras, “Among Wolves,” in which Mr. Rodríguez appeared.

Mr. Rodríguez faced doubts over the years, but his story fascinated many. Mr. Janer became convinced after visiting places Mr. Rodríguez said he had been and meeting people — including a seminarian who had cared for him — who backed up the story and spoke of Mr. Rodríguez’s complete lack of social know-how.

In Rante, a village in San Cibrao das Viñas, in northwest Spain, where Mr. Rodríguez lived for the last quarter-century of his life, some people told Germany’s public broadcaster around the time the film was released that they had doubted his story until it was made into a movie — and some said they continued to be dubious. In 2010, a team from Spain’s public broadcaster traveled with Mr. Rodríguez to the place where he said he had lived, filming him showing some of his survival skills, like catching fish using rocks, and his deep familiarity with nature, including mimicking bird calls.

In any case, he eventually came to be known as the “wolf boy of Sierra Morena” and stuck to the story over the decades.

Claims of having grown up in the wild are widely viewed with skepticism, and expertise in the subject is rare. There have been some notable cases, though they are few. Feral children also appeared in ancient myths and medieval folk tales, fueling a real-life fascination with them.

In 1726, Caroline, the Princess of Wales, sought the guardianship of a youth found in the woods in Germany who became known as Peter the Wild Boy and was a source of wonder in Europe. She installed him in her house in London under the watch of a doctor, then put him in the care of a servant when he proved unruly. The so-called Wild Boy of Aveyron was found in France at the end of the 18th century and was taken to a physician in Paris who tried and failed to teach him society’s ways.

Such tales have intrigued people because they say as much about society as they do about the children said to have lived outside of it. “Through the stories, factual and fictional, of the feral children, there emerges, perhaps, another narrative: the fragmented and haunting story of our continuing relationship with the savage image of ourselves,” the cultural historian Michael Newton wrote in his 2002 book, “Savage Girls and Wild Boys: A History of Feral Children.”

As Mr. Rodríguez told it, he was born into a poor family in southern Spain in June 1946. His mother died when he was very young, and the woman his father later married was an abusive stepmother. The family lived in a remote alpine hut in the Sierra Morena mountain range, turning firewood into charcoal. When he was about 7, he said, he was put in the care of an old goatherd, to be trained to replace him.

“He takes Marcos in and teaches him how to survive, how to care for the flock of goats, how to do everything that might help him,” Mr. Janer said in the 2010 interview.

The old man then died or disappeared, and young Marcos began to fend for himself, unwilling or unable to return to his former home.

Mr. Rodríguez said he lived in the wild for about 11 years with the help of wolves and other animals. In 1965, he was discovered by law enforcement authorities among wolves, wearing animal skins.

He described his return to life among humans as something he did not know how to manage and would never fully embrace. According to Mr. Rodríguez’s interviews and Mr. Janer’s study, his rehabilitation was undertaken by nuns. He said he had lost the habits of walking upright and of using human speech, and he had forgotten how to behave with people.

Mr. Rodríguez said he struggled with human society for much of his life. Employers had taken advantage of him over the years, people had mocked him and he had been happiest among the animals, he said in interviews.

In Rante, he worked with Amigas das Árbores, an environmental group, speaking to children at schools about his youth and his unique experience with animals.

The group, in a post on social media earlier this month, said that one of his final wishes had been “for his ashes to remain in the village that took him in.”

In an interview with the newspaper El País in 2018, Mr. Rodríguez said that despite his disappointment with humanity, he had no chance of returning to a life in the mountains. The area where he had once lived now featured cottages connected to the electric grid, and the wolves were strangers.

“If I call out to them they are going to respond, but they are not going to approach me,” he said. “I smell like people.”

item.title: U.S. Tariffs Could Price Canadian Firms Out of U.S. and Threaten Thousands of Jobs
item.description:
The 50 percent tariffs that President Trump imposed on Canada this weekend could be devastating for many Canadian companies and their employees. It could price them out of the United States and lead to the loss in tens of thousands of jobs, economists say.

“Fifty percent is a huge number for the individual products that are affected,” said Joseph Steinberg, a professor of macroeconomics at the University of Toronto.

“For those products, we should see a very large reduction in exports,” he added. “In some cases, exports will stop altogether, and the firms that produce those products will be severely impacted. Some will undoubtedly shut down.”

Up to 90,000 jobs in Canada could be lost, according to calculations by Trevor Tombe, a trade economist at the University of Calgary in Alberta. Those include jobs at companies not directly affected by tariffs. For example, demand for truck drivers will dry up once Canadian firms are shut out of the U.S. market.

Among the industries likely to be hit hard is forestry. After decades of steep tariffs on softwood lumber — levies that Mr. Trump increased last year — it is facing additional 50 percent tariffs on exports that include plywood, laminated wood products, fiberboard, paper, tissue for toilet paper and packaging.

“We’re getting hammered,” said Derek Nighbor, president of the Forest Products Association of Canada. Nevertheless, he said, he supports the decision of Prime Minister Mark Carney to walk away from trade negotiations with the United States on Friday night.

“This is at a time when the fundamentals of the U.S. economy are not great,” Mr. Nighbor added. “We’re dealing with very, very soft markets that aren’t going to get much better if this kind of tariff behavior keeps up.”

On Tuesday, Mr. Carney is expected to announce retaliation tariffs against the United States, Canadian officials said.

The collapse of trade talks led Mr. Trump to unleash the new tariffs on hundreds of exports from Canada. They cover about $20 billion in trade from Canada. The tariffs arrived on top of levies of 50 percent imposed on Canadian steel and aluminum, as well as 25 percent duties on automobiles that Mr. Trump announced last year.

On Monday, Mr. Trump also threatened to raise auto tariffs to 50 percent on Jan. 1 and to impose the same tariff on auto parts that are currently exempted from payments if they qualify as North American under the trade treaty between the United States, Mexico and Canada.

While $20 billion in trade sounds huge, it is about 5.5 percent of the value of all products Canada sends to the United States. So the new tariffs may not have a sweeping, debilitating effect on Canada’s economy, economists say.

Canada’s exports are dominated by shipments of oil and gas — items that Mr. Trump has excluded from his tariff war, along with the fertilizer potash and most minerals.

For the Canadian economy as a whole, the new levies will increase the effective tariff rate for Canadian products by about 2.5 percentage points, economists say. That will raise the average tariff that the United States puts on Canadian goods to about 6.5 percent, Professor Tombe said by email.

By comparison, Mr. Trump negotiated deals with several other major trading partners that brought in 15 percent in general tariffs.

The Royal Bank of Canada also estimated that tariffs at that average level would affect only about 0.4 percent of Canada’s economic output.

But in an analysis published on Monday, TD Securities, Toronto-Dominion Bank’s investment brokerage, said that the new tariffs were a potential problem even if they were unlikely to put sustained pressure on the Canadian dollar.

“The larger concern is the signal a failed agreement sends about the prospects for a broader trade resolution,” the analysis said. “Markets may interpret this as evidence that trade uncertainty will persist.”

While the tariffs that were imposed on Saturday will hurt the forest industries, they will most severely hit companies that export machinery and electronics, and that produce furniture, toys and products made largely of plastic.

The new tariffs will make it impossible for many Canadian companies to continue to sell to the U.S. market, Professor Steinberg said. About 15 percent of Canada’s economy is directly linked to trade with the United States, he estimated. The U.S. market takes about 70 percent of all Canadian exports.

But the importance of selling to Americans varies wildly among Canadian companies and economic sectors. Upward of 90 percent of vehicles made in Canada, for example, go to American buyers.

Mr. Carney, an economist and a former central banker, has pledged 28 billion Canadian dollars, about $20 billion, to help Canadian companies affected by the new U.S. levies, although details have yet to be released.

On Saturday, he suggested that Canada’s debt would not be caught up in a situation like the current instability in the U.S. bond market.

“We are entering a phase where fiscal strength, discipline, focus, is going to be very important; it’s going to be scrutinized,” he told reporters.

“The way the world works is that markets sometimes ignore these fundamentals. And then all of a sudden they focus on them. And when they focus them, if you don’t have your house in order, it is too late. We have our house in order.”

The prime minister also vowed, after the trade talks fell apart, to match the U.S. tariffs “dollar for dollar” on American goods coming into Canada.

Professor Steinberg said it was impossible to impose retaliatory tariffs that had no consequences, like higher prices, for Canadians.

“Canadian retaliatory tariffs on America, they do hurt America a little bit but also hurt the Canadian economy far more,” he said “Tariffs in either direction have roughly 10 times more impact on Canadian economy. That applies to Trump’s tariffs, that applies our retaliatory measures.”

More broadly, he said, tariffs aren’t obviously effective. The retaliatory levies Canada imposed on American-made autos and other products last year did not stop Mr. Trump from introducing his latest tariffs or overtly damage the overall U.S. economy.

“It’s just going to be a cost for the Canadian economy, but what do we gain from doing that?” Professor Steinberg said. “The case simply has not been made to me.”

On Monday, there were no obvious signs of panic in Canada. The S&P/TSX Index of Canadian stocks closed slightly up from last Friday. The Canadian dollar also closed down by less than 1 cent relative to the U.S. dollar.

item.title: Silence, Wolves and the Wild East: Hiking in Portugal’s Côa Valley
item.description:
The flashlight flicks on and carvings appear out of the darkness. They are 20,000 years old. Engravings of ibex, horses and aurochs, drawn alone or in groups. A few are in movement, like ancient animations. Their crisp lines feel timeless.

I am here to walk as much as I can of Portugal’s Côa Valley Grand Route, staying in bed-and-breakfasts and trying to understand the changes that are drawing both wildlife and people back to one of the country’s most remote corners.

I began a week earlier, driving three hours inland from Porto — past crowds of tour buses and day-trippers in the wine region of Pinhão. Evening fell over the vines, and the lights flicked out one by one until the road wound dark and silent through the hills. I watched a stone marten cross the road, low and dark, satin fur.

My first stop is in the village of Vale da Senhora da Póvoa, where Samuel Ribeiro and Marta Simoes, young transplants from Lisbon, run a grocery store and a small nature guiding company. The couple is part of a small wave of people reversing a 50-year tide that has almost entirely emptied this region, as people fled in search of better economic opportunities. Their store, full of both basics and local artisanal products, is about community as much as commerce.

Marta packs me a picnic — crisp local bread, honey, sweet tomatoes in olive oil, plump cherries — and I set off to find the source of the river.

When I find it, the Côa River wells implausibly out of dry ground among oaks and pines, then runs north along the Spanish border. The area, called the Malcata, is a nature reserve of hills and steep valleys that was the last home to wild Iberian lynx in Portugal before they disappeared, and where many hope to see their return.

From my accommodation at Moinho do Maneio, I hike through stands of oak and strawberry trees. A roe deer barks in alarm. Lush ferns reach past my waist and dozens of yellow butterflies lift and flutter as I walk. An abandoned mill appears through the trees. I feel as if I have somehow stepped out of the present, out of Portugal, even out of Europe, and into an enchanted, parallel world.

It is very still. Only the sound of the stream and the birds.

I stop at a farm on the edge of the reserve. Huge dogs with spiked collars wait by the house. Their job is to protect livestock from the wolves that have crept back into this landscape as people have left.

Albano Alavedra, the owner of the farm, offers me a beer. We sit on the terrace under an ancient oak and talk about wolves.

“Wolves make good shepherds,” he says. And good shepherds pay attention to the land, which helps both his animals and the landscape. Where there are wolves, there is no excess of anything, he says. “It is the human who throws it out of balance.”

I ask Mr. Alavedra, who grew up here, why he stayed when so many left. “My mother wanted me to get a degree,” he smiles. But his passion, he says, has always been for farming and for nature. “Only those who really liked it, stayed,” he says. “We are the only ones here now.”

Farther north, the trail crosses a medieval bridge, once the border with Spain. I stop in the evening light as martins and swallows swoop in the gloaming.

In the village of Vilar Maior, Bárbara Cardoso, an engineer and beekeeper, is visiting her elderly mother, Maria Cândida, who runs a bed-and-breakfast in their old family home. Ms. Cardoso welcomes me in and, in the morning, shows me her bees. “I like their determination,” she says. It feels like a metaphor for the whole landscape.

Dinner at the bed-and-breakfast is three courses of local cheese and honey, chickpea stew, ripe tomatoes in salt and olive oil, local wine, then dessert and several glasses of Maria Cândida’s homemade liqueur. I’m chided for not having thirds. We lack a common language, so I can only mime that I’m about to burst. She mimes back that I should eat more, then run uphill to the castle — built to defend the region against Spain. I take her advice, heading up the cobblestone streets. Each stone of the fortress is carved with the symbol of the man who made it, which is apparently how your pay was calculated if you were a stonemason in 13th-century Portugal.

Rewilding Portugal, a nonprofit conservation organization, manages tracts of land in the valley as part of an ambitious plan to accelerate the rewilding already underway. This includes reintroducing species like Sorraia horses, a local breed, and tauros, a specially bred bovine — a modern attempt to recreate the ancient and extinct aurochs, which once roamed across Europe.

Near Vilar Maior, I look for Sorraia horses. Merlin, the bird app on my phone, identifies the songs of 38 different species.

I sit on a granite boulder for breakfast. Sheep cheese on crunchy bread. The sun just cresting the ridge behind me and pushing the morning chill from the air in one hot breath. It is very still, just as it has been for days. There are signs of people everywhere — roads, stone barns, crumbling walls. But I see no one.

I catch movement in the tall grass. Something big. Not a horse. More like a dog. It is an odd feeling to want something to be a wolf while also feeling a chill of unease.

They tell stories about wolves here. That wolves steal the children, leaving only their shoes. They tell old stories, and new ones too. That environmentalists are sneaking wolves into the towns and releasing them at night. None is true.

I look again, and a family of boar snuffle out of the brush, in search of their own breakfast. There goes my wolf story.

When I find horses, it is unexpected. They trot down the path, eyeing me uncertainly, then prance away among the wildflowers, sleek and gray. A booted eagle looks sharply down from her nest as storks and buzzards soar overhead.

Farther north, I arrive at a bend in the river as evening falls and swim in the cool water. Afterward, a pair of otters appear, silky and dark in the fading light. Uphill, in the garden of Côa Honeycomb, my hotel, a cat twists around my feet. Not quite a lynx.

Fernando Romão, who runs Wildlife Portugal, a nature guiding company, takes me to look for tauros in the morning. Originally from Lisbon, Mr. Romão moved here and became obsessed with the region’s biodiversity. He is a gold mine of information about everything from rare plants to insects and wildlife, including a water snake — as richly patterned as a Persian carpet — that he points out in a stream.

We pass an ancient “wolf trap,” evidence of the region’s long and complex history with predators. (A sacrificial lamb would be left inside the stone enclosure as bait to trap.) We cut across granite boulders, brambles scratching at our legs and arms, the Côa far below.

I ask about tourism. There isn’t much, he says. People come to see birds and wildlife. Some have a hard time sleeping because they’re unaccustomed to so much silence, he says.

We round a bend and come suddenly upon a herd of tauros. They’re enormous, some weighing more than 2,000 pounds, wild and intimidating with their long horns. Together with Sorraia horses, tauros are transforming the landscape, eating and stamping and allowing oak forests — cleared for agriculture — to return. Conservationists hope that ibex and lynx will soon join them.

Later, Conceição Matos and her husband show me their farm, with accommodation downstairs and her stately family home above. Every room tells a story. One room, she tells me, was hand-painted by a French soldier who stayed during the Napoleonic wars. We descend stone steps into fields where last summer’s fires burned right up to the walls. I’m invited to dinner on the terrace. Bread and olive oil infused with thyme and rosemary from the fields, and “garden sardines” — vegetables battered and cooked as fish would be on the coast. Crisp white wine and water with a hint of fresh vervain.

Even more than the fires, Ms. Matos tells me their challenge is finding people to work. “I still believe a lot of people will come back,” she says, looking out over the cherry trees and the fields that her family has farmed for generations.

At last, the Côa nears the Douro River, where the trail ends beside the Côa Museum, overlooking the vineyards. As I get closer, my hopes of seeing a lynx or a wolf fade, but I still look and listen for howls under the waning moon.

Just south, the trail climbs to avoid a UNESCO World Heritage area that protects prehistoric rock art along the riverbank, accessible only with a guide. As the sun sets, I meet Marco Ferraz, who has run cultural and nature tours here for years and who tells me the best time to visit is at dusk.

As we approach the river, he tells me how this region was once set to be flooded for a dam, and that the discovery of prehistoric engravings became a national election issue. António Guterres, now the United Nations Secretary General, lobbied to save them while running for prime minister, and won.

We walk along the riverbank in darkness. The Côa is unseen but roaring, fed by the many tributaries I’ve crossed since that humble spring in the hills.

When the engravings appear in the flashlight, I sit in awe. Drawings of the deep past, but also now — as wildlife returns to the valley — of the present.

item.title: Australia Bans Generative A.I. From Official Music Charts
item.description:
Songs that are wholly or largely created by generative A.I. will be banned from Australia’s music charts under new rules announced on Tuesday, but recordings that use the technology in a supporting role will still be allowed.

The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA), which oversees the charts of the country’s most popular music, said the changes will apply from Friday.

The move follows a global push by the music industry and authorities to create clearer regulation around A.I. use in music and ensure appropriate copyright protections for original artists.

ARIA’s chief executive officer, Annabelle Herd, said the music charts should reflect what Australians are listening to, but a chart that rewarded A.I. output would “undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent.”

Many artists use A.I. tools, and music charts should “keep room for that,” Ms. Herd said in a statement released by ARIA. “But music generated wholesale by services built on artists’ recordings is a different matter.”

Under the changes, recordings developed using generative A.I. will only be allowed if they are “substantially human-made” and do not raise “stream or chart manipulation concerns,” the statement said.

For example, if a song’s lead vocal or key instrumental performance is generated by A.I., the track would be ineligible, ARIA said. But a human lead vocal with A.I. backing vocals would be allowed.

Under the rules, ARIA may remove a recording from the charts if it is deemed ineligible, although artists will be allowed to appeal the decision. A.I.-generated recordings will also not qualify for the ARIA Awards — the country’s top music industry prize.

The Australian musician Ben Lee, who is known for hits like “Cigarettes Will Kill You” and “Catch My Disease,” said non-generative A.I. was used by artists in the process of music production, including for pitch correction and noise reduction. But generative A.I. and its impacts on the industry needed to be looked at more closely, he said.

“I’m not the kind of person who is at all fundamentally opposed to technological changes in my industry,” he said. “It feels like healthy pushback is a really vital part of us looking responsibly at the way to integrate these technologies into our industries.”

“I don’t see this as the endpoint. I see this as the start of a conversation,” Mr. Lee said of the chart changes.

Alexis Weaver, a composer and lecturer at the Sydney Conservatorium of Music, said ARIA’s move was a “wonderful step forward” in valuing human creativity.

The discussion about the use of A.I. in music is “exceptionally fraught and very emotional for a lot of musicians and so everyone will have a different opinion,” she told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.

The changes come just months after a chart-topping cover of Madonna’s “Like a Prayer” angered some in the music industry who believed it was produced with A.I., the network reported this year.

The song, which has been streamed more than 48 million times on Spotify, was later updated on the music platform to include A.I. credits, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported.

Oliver Bown, a University of New South Wales professor studying the impacts of A.I. on the creative industries, said ARIA was the latest in a long line of organizations to develop policies banning some level of A.I.

“Everyone’s watching everyone else,” he said, pointing to governments, record labels and various music bodies across the world.

For example, the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, which represents the recording industry worldwide, released a set of principles around generative A.I. use and chart eligibility in June. Songs that were wholly generated by A.I. were banned from charts that the federation oversees in Latin America, the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia. ARIA’s changes are based on the foundation’s principles.

British actors, musicians and writers welcomed the government’s decision this year to abandon its plans to let A.I. firms use copyright-protected work without permission. In the United States, a string of court cases has emerged over the misuse of A.I. and copyright.

Mr. Bown said the speed at which generative A.I. models had developed and been adopted was “unprecedented” and had sent shock waves across the broader creative industries.

But he is hopeful that the technology could also be used to create something new: “Once we establish some boundaries between ethical and unethical practices, there’s a great deal of room for people to use A.I., and to do really interesting things with it,” he said.

item.title: Chinese Artist Sentenced to Three Years in Prison for Mao Sculptures
item.description:
A Chinese court on Tuesday sentenced a prominent New York-based artist, Gao Zhen, to three years in prison for making irreverent sculptures of Mao Zedong more than 15 years ago, according to his wife.

The Sanhe City People’s Court in Hebei Province found Mr. Gao guilty of slandering one of the country’s heroes, highlighting the shrinking space for expression under China’s leader, Xi Jinping.

The case of Mr. Gao, who had emigrated to the United States and was detained in Beijing two years ago while visiting family, underlined the opacity of China’s legal system. The 70-year-old artist was tried during a one-day secret hearing in March that his family and U.S. diplomats were barred from attending. He was found guilty and sentenced during Tuesday’s hearing, which two of Mr. Gao’s other brothers were able to attend.

Mr. Gao is the elder of the artistic duo known as the Gao Brothers, who became famous during the early 2000s for their satirical and provocative takes on politically sensitive topics such as the Cultural Revolution, a decade of political turmoil unleashed by Mao, as well as the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre.

The three-year sentence, the maximum Mr. Gao could have received, means that he will serve one more year in prison after two years’ detention. The artist plans to appeal the court’s decision.

Gao Qiang, Mr. Gao’s younger brother, who lives in New York and who worked with him on the Mao sculptures, said in a Facebook post before the sentencing that whatever the court decides, “history will ultimately judge the larger question: Whether an artist can be imprisoned for confronting history through art.”

“Gao Zhen has already lost nearly two years of freedom. He should go home,” Gao Qiang added.

Gao Zhen was arrested at his art studio on the outskirts of Beijing while visiting China in 2024. When his wife, Zhao Yaliang, tried to take the couple’s 7-year-old son, a U.S. citizen, back to the United States, she was barred from leaving. The two have remained in China, waiting for Mr. Gao’s release. Mr. Gao has refused to confess or plead guilty, according to Ms. Zhao.

The Gao brothers rose to prominence at a time of relative openness in China. While the police shut down their exhibitions, the two were able to continue working and became known for their creative antics while evading the authorities. They held underground art exhibitions and in the case of one especially provocative sculpture — a bronze statue of Mao kneeling in repentance, called “Mao’s Guilt” — they kept the head of the sculpture separate, bringing it out only for special viewings.

According to Ms. Zhao, that piece is one of three that prosecutors named in their evidence against Mr. Gao. The other two included a sculpture of Mao with breasts and a Pinocchio nose, and another that depicts a group of Mao likenesses with guns, preparing to execute Jesus.

Criticism of Mao, the former Chinese leader whose legacy is considered central to the legitimacy of the Chinese Communist Party, is strictly controlled. As part of a campaign to enforce the Party’s version of history, China has made it illegal to tarnish the reputation of historical figures or to question official narratives.

Mr. Gao was charged under that slander law, which was passed in 2018, years after he produced the sculptures of Mao. Journalists, stand-up comedians and regular citizens have been punished under the same law, but Mr. Gao’s case is one of the first times that it has been used retroactively.

People familiar with the case said Mr. Gao had been accused of disseminating images of the Mao sculptures online as recently as 2024, including on the cover of a biography of the former leader by a Chinese journalist who emigrated to the United States in the 1980s.

Shane Yi, a researcher at the nonprofit Chinese Human Rights Defenders, said that by targeting Mr. Gao, the Chinese authorities were able to remind overseas Chinese citizens that the state still had power over them whether they are abroad or back in China.

“But no matter which motive carries the most weight: A person has been locked up for two years over his art, and his wife and young son, a U.S. citizen, have been barred from leaving China this entire time,” he said.

Ms. Zhao said that her husband had been punished while in prison, including being deprived of food, and being barred from reading books and getting letters from his family.

Still, Mr. Gao has continued to make art, tearing pieces of plain paper to make portraits of his family. In a recent letter to his wife, Mr. Gao enclosed a poem: “Sleepless nights, tossing and turning, memories drift like clouds and smoke/Once a dragon slayer, now imprisoned, he has no regrets for mocking the wicked.”

Pei-Lin Wu contributed reporting.

item.title: Mass Mortality and Infected Mammals: Australia’s Bird Flu Fears Come True
item.description:
Bird flu is sweeping across Australia, devastating its unique birds and mammals, many of which are found nowhere else in the world.

Already, mass mortality events have killed more than 1,000 birds, and the disease has crossed into seals. Experts fear more deaths are likely.

Australia confirmed its first case of H5N1 in June in a migratory brown skua, a sub-Antarctic species on the country’s southern coast. Since then, the disease has rapidly spread.

To date, there have been 309 confirmed bird flu events, official data shows (the country is not counting individual bird cases, instead referring to events that could include one or more birds). Among the bird species to have died are greater crested terns, sea gulls and little penguins.

The state of South Australia has been the worst-hit, recording 194 events. More than 1,000 crested terns — a large coastal bird with a yellow bill — are believed to have died from the disease on three remote islands, the state’s leader said last week.

On Monday, the environment minister, Murray Watt, told the national broadcaster: “We are likely to see mass mortalities of birds and mammals. And I know that is a very distressing thing for Australians to hear, but we also need to be realistic.”

So far, the disease has not been detected in poultry or on farms, according to the government, and the risk to humans remains low. People who come across affected animals have been told not to touch them, but to photograph and report the sighting via official hotlines.

Euan Ritchie, a professor of wildlife ecology at Deakin University, said that while the disease had not been in Australia long, the speed of its spread was concerning.

“We have a feeling of dread that we’re only about to see the beginning of it now and it’s about to get far worse,” he said.

He added that Australia’s wildlife had evolved in isolation for millions of years, creating animals found nowhere else, such as the Australian sea lion, which is considered vulnerable, with fewer than 10,000 adults in the wild.

But this isolation also meant that the animals were more at risk of contracting new pathogens because they had not developed any immunity. This particular strain of bird flu has decimated animal populations worldwide since 2020. While Australia has had other strains of bird flu before, it successfully eradicated them. The arrival of H5N1 this year marks the first time Australia has experienced the disease, which is putting the country’s response to the test.

The Australian government began vaccinating at-risk bird species this month. Among those receiving the vaccination will be 5,000 little penguins in the state of Victoria. They are easy to vaccinate because they waddle from the ocean to their burrows each evening.

Millions in funding have also been allocated to combat the disease, including increased surveillance to ensure early detection and response.

But some conservationists and experts have criticized the government for being too slow to roll out vaccines and have called for increased investment in habitat protections.

Ariful Islam, a bird flu and epidemiology expert from Charles Sturt University, said vaccinations were not a “silver bullet,” particularly when it came to wild birds, which needed monitoring to ensure that the vaccine produced the necessary antibodies for protection from the disease.

The public is also joining the fight.

Volunteers are helping document bird deaths, particularly in South Australia. Among them is Maureen Christie, secretary of Friends of Shorebirds SE, who spends each morning searching for sick or dead birds along a patch of coastline in the town of Carpenter Rocks, and reporting them.

But the work has taken its toll.

“You can’t do anything to really help the birds,” she said.

On Monday morning, she was “elated” to find only 11 sick or dead birds. A few weeks ago, at one location, there were carcasses every few footsteps.

Yes. H5N1 has infected a range of mammals, including cows, cats, foxes and raccoons around the world. But marine mammals have been particularly hard hit. The disease killed at least 24,000 South American sea lions along the continent’s coasts in less than a year in 2023.

In Australia, authorities confirmed the first case of H5N1 in a long-nosed fur seal in South Australia last week. A second seal was suspected to have died from the disease on Monday.

Seal expert Jane Younger, from the University of Tasmania, said the disease could become an “extinction event” if it were to spread among marine mammals such as the Australian sea lion. Most of the sea lions share the same habitat in South Australia as the infected birds.

A vaccine has not yet been approved for use in Australian mammals.

“Unfortunately, there’s not really anything that can be done to stop the virus from spreading,” Ms. Younger said, adding, “it’s spread by wild animals, and we just don’t have any control over that.”

item.title: Christian Convert Who Fled Iran and Was Ousted From U.S. Finds a New Home
item.description:
The young woman became the face of migrants deported by the United States to Panama. She was locked up in a hotel, detained in a camp in the Darién jungle and stranded in a country where she knew neither the language nor anyone else. Later, she lent her name to a bill in Congress aimed at providing more protection to some migrants seeking asylum in the United States.

The woman, Artemis Ghasemzadeh, a 28-year-old Iranian Christian convert, has now found a home — in Canada. In June, the Canadian government granted her asylum, a happy bookend to her nearly two-year journey fleeing religious persecution in Iran only to get entangled in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Ms. Ghasemzadeh arrived on Denman Island near Vancouver in early July with few belongings other than clothes. But her heart, she said, was filled with gratitude and hope for a new beginning.

“I’m still kind of in shock. I can’t believe I’m really here and this is not a dream,” Ms. Ghasemzadeh said in a telephone interview. “I can finally say the struggle is over.”

Ms. Ghasemzadeh left Iran for Mexico in December 2024 with her brother, Shahin, also a Christian covert, and entered the United States by jumping over a wall on the southern border. Border patrol officers caught and transferred them to detention facilities, separating them. In February 2025, she was shackled and put on a U.S. military plane heading to Panama.

That flight was the Trump administration’s first experiment with deporting migrants to a third country, meaning a place where they are not citizens. Since then, third-country flights have gone to at least 18 countries including Costa Rica, El Salvador and the Central African Republic, among others. The Trump administration, despite its acute hostility toward Iran’s government, has nonetheless worked with it to send at least two deportation flights directly to Iran.

For Ms. Ghasemzadeh, the prospect of being sent back to Iran was terrifying. Iran’s law considers leaving Islam for another faith as blasphemy, punishable by death. Christians born to the faith are free to practice but converts attend secret underground churches and prayer groups to evade arrest and persecution.

“I wanted to live freely, to live without fear, to live without someone wanting to kill me,” Ms. Ghasemzadeh said in an interview in 2025.

After Ms. Ghasemzadeh and her fellow deportees were flown out of the United States, Panama had locked them in a hotel in Panama City and later transported them in the middle of the night to a migrant detention camp in the Darién jungle, where they were held for weeks.

Ms Ghasemzadeh had a singular role in drawing the world’s attention to their plight. She made a social media video that went viral and with her smuggled cellphone provided updates to The New York Times. The coverage gained wide attention, including from Christian advocacy organizations and rights activists. A group of high-profile immigration lawyers took on the case pro bono and won the deportees’ release from jungle detention.

Panama, facing lawsuits and an international uproar, granted the deportees a 90-day humanitarian visa. Many eventually left Panama, but Ms. Ghasemzadeh decided to stay and search for a legal path to North America. She hoped to be reunited with her brother, who was granted asylum in the United States this year and now lives in Texas.

In May 2025, Representative Yassamin Ansari, a Democrat from Arizona who is Iranian American, introduced legislation in Congress called the Artemis Act. The bill sought to prohibit the expedited removal of individuals fleeing countries that the State Department says persecute religious minorities and to ensure they have the chance to claim asylum in a U.S. immigration court. The legislation had widespread support from Democrats but faced opposition from Republicans, who hold the majority in the House.

Lawyers said they told Ms. Ghasemzadeh that the chances of the United States reversing its decision and allowing her back were slim given the political climate around the immigration issue.

Immigrating to Canada presented its own challenges. The country had a quota for refugees and required a Canadian citizen to sponsor their applications. She did not know anyone in Canada.

Meanwhile, Ms. Ghasemzadeh said, she tried to build a life in Panama City. She found a church, learned Spanish, made friends and worked as a dental hygienist.

In Canada, Ian and Naomi Elliot, a retired couple who run programs for their local Afghan refugee community, read a profile of Ms. Ghasemzadeh in The Times anddecided to sponsor her asylum application. The couple said they had helped an Afghan and an Ethiopian secure asylum in Canada.

“I couldn’t sleep after reading the article. I thought this is a Christian sister who shares our faith and is paying a massive price for this belief,” said Mr. Elliot, 68, who works with InterVarsity Christian Fellowship and is a community leader at their small church on Denman Island.

The Elliots undertook a monthslong effort, contacting Canadian officials, refugee aid agencies and activists, while consulting lawyers in three different countries. The couple prayed for her every night. But “everywhere we tried, the door was shut,” said Mr. Elliot, because Canada’s quota for privately sponsored refugees in 2025 had been filled and there was a long waiting list.

Then shortly before Christmas, they said, they received an unexpected call. City of Refugees, an agency that facilitates the resettlement of persecuted Christians in Canada, called Mr. Elliot. The agency had a cancellation and would give the spot to Ms. Ghasemzadeh.

The agency gave Mr. Elliot 48 hours to submit her paperwork, find a church to sponsor her and put up $25,000. The first two tasks were easy, but coming up with the money on short notice was difficult. He called an American lawyer in Texas who had helped Ms. Ghasemzadeh’s brother, and although the two had never met, the lawyer wired money to Mr. Elliot’s bank account.

Ms. Ghasemzadeh had only a few days to get ready for her departure, she said.

“The first thing I thought was that I don’t have to worry about getting displaced again,” she recalled. “I can finally get my own place and not live in shelters. I want to go to university and study dental hygiene or dentistry, and then travel freely without fear.”

In Canada, the Elliots were preparing for her arrival, outfitting her future bedroom with a desk, chair, mirror and a green plant, as well as new sheets and curtains. They also bought her a bathing suit, which she would need for summering on the island.

“Big hearts make a huge difference. It all worked out like a miracle,” said Naomi Elliot, 65, who said her parents and grandparents survived the Holocaust in Europe and later migrated to Canada.

On the day of her arrival, Mr. Elliot and his friends drove excitedly to the nearby airport, while Ms. Elliot stayed home to prepare a lunch feast. They brought flowers, gifts and signs that said “Welcome Artemis” in English and Persian.

When she arrived, Ms. Ghasemzadeh ran to Mr. Elliot and hugged him tightly. “Thank you for saving my life,” she told him. They both cried.

item.title: U.S. Removes Syria From Its List of Terrorism Sponsors
item.description:
The United States has lifted the last of its crippling economic sanctions on Syria after the Treasury Department removed the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.

The move was welcomed on Tuesday by Syrian officials, who view it as a crucial step toward reconstruction after the end of the country’s brutal civil war of nearly 14 years.

“Great people of Syria, you have done it again,” President Ahmed al-Sharaa of Syria said, in comments carried by Syrian state media. “Sanctions have been lifted and restrictions removed. I ask God to help us serve you.”

The United States designated Syria a state sponsor of terror in the late 1970s, when the country was ruled by the dictator Hafez al-Assad, largely because of his regime’s support for Palestinian armed groups.

Additional U.S. sanctions were imposed during the rule of Mr. al-Assad’s son and successor, Bashar al-Assad. He was ousted in December 2024, during the civil war, by a coalition of rebel factions led by Mr. al-Sharaa.

The fall of the Assad regime left Syrians optimistic about the country’s economic prospects and hoping for a quick reintegration into the global market under an interim government. Yet that recovery has been slow and bumpy, hampered in part by lingering U.S. sanctions.

In recent months, Syrians have faced high inflation and rising food and fuel prices that have stoked discontent with the government.

The removal of the state sponsor of terror designation on Monday came after a U.S. congressional review process and after Syria joined the Global Coalition to Defeat the Islamic State, according to the State Department. The United States also revoked the terrorism designation for Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, a rebel group that was headed by Mr. al-Sharaa and that was previously known as the Al Nusra Front, the State Department said.

The United States had already removed other punitive sanctions that had been imposed on Syria during the civil war.

Last year, during a trip to Saudi Arabia where he met with Mr. al-Sharaa, President Trump announced that his administration would lift sanctions on Syria to give the country “a chance” to rebuild.

In December, Mr. Trump signed a law repealing the 2019 Caesar Act, which imposed severe financial restrictions on Syria’s economy in an effort to hold the Assad government accountable for its atrocities. The act was named after a photographer who had smuggled out images depicting torture in Syrian prisons.

Still, Syrian and foreign businesses and investors have been wary of returning to the country, citing uncertainties over the interim government’s fiscal policies and concerns about security.

Last year, when Syria made its first electronic transfer with a Western bank since the end of the civil war, it was hailed as a key step for the country to rejoin the global banking system. Yet the Syrian economy remains mostly cash based and international credit cards are rarely accepted.

The U.S. special envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, said on Monday that the rescinding of the state sponsor of terror designation was “another decisive step in Syria’s remarkable journey from isolation to partnership, and from a source of terrorism to a committed partner in the global fight against it.”

“For too long, this designation was another wall separating the Syrian people from the investment, enterprise, and opportunity necessary to rebuild their nation,” he added, in a post on social media. “Today, another wall comes down.”

Syrian officials hope that the end of U.S. sanctions may help the country attract foreign capital.

Analysts say that Syria’s ports on the Mediterranean Sea could become an export route for oil and gas shipments from the region, and a possible alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway in the Persian Gulf that has been effectively closed since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

To take advantage of those opportunities, Syria needs to rebuild and modernize roads, utilities and infrastructure that were destroyed during the war — all of which require partner states and international investment.

item.title: Tornado Rips Through Towns in Southern France
item.description:
An unusually strong tornado tore through southwestern France, ripping up roofs and leaving dozens of people injured, the authorities said on Tuesday.

“A tornado of rare intensity struck Aude late yesterday afternoon,” Laurent Nuñez, the French interior minister, said on social media, referring to a prefecture in the Occitanie region.

The tornado arrived on Monday, battering towns and villages in the area, according to Météo-France, the national weather agency. At least 39 people were injured, two of whom were in critical condition, Emmanuelle Plantier-Lemarchand, secretary general of the Aude prefecture, said. The regional authorities issued a warning, but the direction had been hard to forecast, Ms. Plantier-Lemarchand told the French broadcaster Ici Occitanie.

“The phenomenon that struck us was an intense, violent and traumatic phenomenon, but it was difficult to predict,” Ms. Plantier-Lemarchand noted. While there were no reports of anyone missing, firefighters were combing the region for potential victims, the authorities said.

While tornadoes occur across France every year, particularly in the northwest and along the Mediterranean coasts, they are usually relatively weak and small. That also makes them hard to forecast. On Monday, Météo-France issued an orange alert, the second-highest warning, saying that conditions could lead to a “potential swirling phenomenon.” Wind up to 75 miles per hour, hail and thunderstorms had also been expected.

The town of Pomas, which has a population of about 1,000, suffered the worst of the tornado. Fifteen people were hospitalized and 300 homes there were damaged, the authorities said. Heeding the warnings, many residents had taken shelter in a community center, while others sought refuge with relatives or friends in neighboring towns.

“When the wind started picking up, we went to take cover, and then it was like machine-gun fire, roof tiles flying everywhere, rocks and everything,” one resident told the broadcaster France 2. The Pomas municipality urged residents to stay away from their homes as more than 120 firefighters worked to clear the wreckage.

The mayor of Pomas, Hervé Giné, told Ici Occitanie that it was a “true miracle” that the town had recorded no deaths.

“Yes, the material damage is very hard to take; it’s painful,” he added. “Some lost everything they had.”

The tornado knocked out power across 10 towns in the region, leaving about 2,800 households without electricity. By Tuesday, the power had been restored to around half of those homes.

Farther south, hail storms pelted riders competing in La Vuelta, a cross-country cycling race, forcing them to take shelter, organizers said. They added that Stage 3 of the race had been canceled because of extreme weather.

Nazaneen Ghaffar contributed reporting.

item.title: What Happened to the Coveted Western Tanks Sent to Ukraine?
item.description:
The screens covering a command post wall served up live video feeds from bomber drones, a ground drone trundling down a mud path and surveillance drones scoping out a burning house — a catalog of modern warfare.

One thing missing from the picture were the tanks that gave the 33rd Separate Mechanized Brigade’s battalion its name.

Once Ukraine’s most sought-after Western weapons, tanks now mostly sit idle, hidden in forests and collecting cobwebs. The $10 million machines, procured with great fanfare, proved no match for cheap drones that now dominate the battlefield. Yet Ukraine still maintains them and trains soldiers to use them, while trying to imagine new ways to deploy them.

“We’re making virtually no use of armored vehicles,” Oleksandr Syrskyi, who until last month was Ukraine’s top general, said recently. “This raises the question: How can we neutralize this advantage enjoyed by drones and give our armor a new lease on life?”

That question was at the heart of a clash over war strategy that led General Syrskyi to be relieved of his command last month.

Some of Ukraine’s premier tank divisions are not waiting around for the answer.

Tank crews should not be stagnant, said a fresh-faced commander in the 33rd, who, like most soldiers interviewed, gave only his call sign, Morpheus, in keeping with military protocol. That’s why, he said, he tells his battalion that they need to learn something new.

Ukraine started asking for Western-made tanks almost immediately after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, when they seemed essential. Kyiv’s allies resisted sending them until January 2023, when Britain, Germany and the United States changed course following fraught negotiations and public pressure.

The 33rd Brigade was formed in part to receive those Western tanks. But by the time they entered the fight late that spring, cheap drones were already inflicting a deadly toll and were able to strike tanks at their most vulnerable points.

Russian forces started covering their tanks with anti-drone meshes and cages. “People laughed at them back then, saying they were making BBQ grills,” recalled a tank maintenance chief with the 33rd whose call sign is Energetyk. “But they were heading in the right direction.”

Ukraine followed suit, adding protective cages and reactive armor — external panels that detonate when struck, to deflect attacking munitions — in hopes of maintaining tanks’ relevance.

But soon both sides stopped using heavy armor for assaults.

Tank crews must remain ready, said a company commander, call sign Fin, so his men stay busy training, maintaining the tanks and welding on new protections. In combat or not, there is no rest, said Fin, 26, fiddling with the Virgin Mary charm on his black rope bracelet.

The 33rd carries out live-fire exercises every two weeks or so, to keep its skills fresh. One sunny morning, between sunflower fields, troops positioned a tank and set up targets in the distance.

Commanders sat with other soldiers under a makeshift shade, snacking on seeds and sharing a liter of Pepsi.

Yuri Kosenko, 57, had just come off two weeks in a frontline dugout that he said smelled like dampness and mold. There had been no tank fighting but so many “mosquitoes,” he said — rubbing his arm then pointing to the sky to make clear he meant both the biting kind and the exploding kind — that he had to carry a drone detector to the latrine.

Like most soldiers interviewed, he said he was fine without combat engagements because he had seen enough battle. “War is war. There’s nothing to like about it,” the soldier said as shells were loaded into the tank.

Soon the crew climbed in and spun the gun around. The first few rounds were off the mark. Orders went back and forth by radio, requesting adjustments.

Three more shells fired, each setting off a blast that made only half the soldiers flinch.

“You guys missed,” radioed the commander.

“We know — we can see it from here,” a crew member replied.

The Pepsi bottle was nearly empty by that point. A tank driver, Mechan, took out pancakes filled with shredded chicken to share, brought back from his recent leave.

Today Energetyk, 57, works in a forest in the Kharkiv region, well behind the front line. There, birds chirp, the air smells like wood and only upon a close look can camouflage netting be spotted among the trees.

German-made Leopard tanks sit beneath the nets, their turrets turned backward in the “travel position.” Some await repairs or maintenance like oil changes. Others, like one covered in spider webs, are parked in reserve for combat, though those orders have stopped coming.

Energetyk oversaw a crew swapping out the engine of a tank that had hit a mine and caught fire. Another tank had taken a drone strike to the turret, he said, pointing to its parking spot as he set off down a mud track through the woods with ammunition slung over his shoulder.

The damage occurred not during combat but “evacuations,” when tanks towed damaged equipment, effectively acting as extraordinarily expensive tractors.

Even then, said Archie, a gunner smoking a cigarette nearby, the tanks can venture out only in bad weather, when wind, rain and poor visibility mean fewer drones.

With a steadier internet connection, he said, he might spend his newfound downtime learning — maybe improving his German.

Archie, 57, said he would not mind resuming combat missions, but Golden, 27, who was waiting to move a repaired tank to a netted parking spot, said that, for now, he would rather tanks not be used at all.

“I’ve already burned inside a tank — that’s enough for me,” said Golden, laughing uncomfortably as he recounted narrowly surviving that mission.

After the live-fire exercise, the tank driver Mechan and his crew returned to the small house they share, where delicacies made by his wife filled the fridge. He hung up his gun then swapped out sweaty coveralls and dusty boots for shorts and sandals.

Perched on his cot before cooking up a batch of his wife’s potato dumplings, Mechan said that after working on old Soviet T-64 tanks, the switch to Leopards had been a welcome one.

“It is like driving a Mercedes or a BMW,” he said, flashing two thumbs up, but now he drives only rarely, on towing missions. Mechan showed a video of his tank dragging a charred vehicle through a field.

He lamented that his skills might deteriorate without more practice, so the towing mission felt good, even if it was dangerous.

But Dima, whose cot was opposite, questioned the value of using Leopards as tractors, putting both tanks and crews at risk.

“For what? To recover a burned-out vehicle?” he added, incredulous. Better to retrain to fly drones, he said, as Mechan was doing at night, practicing with a console near his cot.

It felt strange and unfamiliar to fly drones, Mechan confessed, but he said the era of tanks is over.

Some newer recruits to the 33rd have never even touched a tank. Among them was Korzhyk, 33, who joined the brigade in 2025 and spends his days repairing ground drones in a dark workshop.

Johnny, 37, a squad commander working alongside him, used to drive tanks but did not hesitate when asked to transfer to this unit using ground drones.

Driving tanks, he said, “you close the hatch, drive out, and have no idea whether you are going to come back.”

Fin, the company commander, insisted that tanks would not remain sidelined, because new technology would allow them to adapt.

Maybe they will be outfitted with A.I. to create protective domes, he suggested, or their own drone interceptors.

But back at the command post, Morpheus said that about half his battalion had retrained as drone operators.

It’s about trying to find ways to use his personnel, Morpheus said, jiggling his leg as he watched the bank of screens.

Getting tanks back into battle would require a major technological breakthrough, he added.

“I’m convinced that tanks still have a future, but there’s one caveat,” Morpheus said, adding, “I think they will be unmanned.”

item.title: U.S. Said to Be Returning Diplomats to Middle East Embassies
item.description:
The State Department is preparing to send U.S. diplomats back to embassies in the Middle East that were evacuated before and during the war with Iran, suggesting that the Trump administration does not anticipate a return to all-out hostilities.

The return of foreign service officers and the scaling back of emergency measures taken at U.S. missions in the Middle East could begin this week, according to an internal State Department document obtained by The Times.

The changes were also described by three U.S. officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk with the press.

The restaffing is set to proceed even though talks between the United States and Iran have floundered, leaving the Trump administration to threaten new economic sanctions.

Embassies slated to restore higher levels of staffing include those in Israel, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Oman, Iraq and Kuwait, the document says.

In a statement, the State Department said it “continuously reviews the security posture at our diplomatic missions around the world. Based on our latest assessment, we are adjusting our staffing posture at certain posts in the Middle East to ensure we can continue advancing U.S. foreign policy objectives while protecting the safety and security of our personnel.”

In late February, a day before the United States and Israel struck Iran, nonessential embassy workers in Jerusalem and their family members were given the option to leave Israel at government expense. Over the following weeks, the State Department issued orders to evacuate missions across the Middle East as Iran and its regional allies targeted U.S. diplomatic outposts in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Iraq and elsewhere in the region with explosive drones and rockets.

Diplomats assigned to some of those countries worked from their homes rather than at embassies as a precaution.

Current and former State Department officials said that redeploying staff signaled an easing of tensions, despite stalled talks between the United States and Iran over extending a 60-day cease-fire that expired last week.

“Returning personnel to missions that were partly evacuated suggests the administration believes the war is winding down,” said Dan Shapiro, who was the U.S. ambassador to Israel during the Obama administration and a Department of Defense official focused on the Middle East during the Biden administration.

The document says the first diplomats to return will be at the U.S. Embassy in Lebanon, though it would not reach full staffing under the plan. Ultimately, the documents say, staff will completely return to three embassies, in Israel, Jordan and Oman.

Posts in the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Lebanon will initially cap staffing at 85 percent, and posts in Iraq, Kuwait and Bahrain at 75 percent. In the six Gulf countries and Lebanon, the State Department will enforce restrictions on bringing family members, the document added.

“The limits on family members in the Gulf suggest that the government still believes there is an elevated risk,” said John R. Bass, the under secretary of state for management during the Biden administration. “They suggest that the threat environment is less than 30, 60, or 90 days ago, but more than before the start of the war.”

Some diplomats who evacuated because of the war had pressed for clarity on where they would be stationed, two of the U.S. officials said — particularly those with children who needed to make placement decisions ahead of the school year. It is unclear how much that pressure influenced the decision, if at all.

Former State Department officials cautioned that returning diplomats and some dependents to the region may signal a desire by the Trump administration to avoid renewed fighting, but it does not guarantee a lasting peace.

“Bringing back embassy staff does not tie their hands for taking action against Iran in the future,” said Robert Danin, a former deputy assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern affairs.

“They did it once,” he said, referring to embassy evacuations earlier this year. “They can do it again.”

item.title: U.S. Campaign on Iran’s Economy May Still Risk Regional Military Escalation
item.description:
Facing a fresh economic assault from the United States, Iran’s leaders are gambling that they can weather the coming storm and make the cost of their suffering felt in an oil-rich region that is critical to the global economy.

As Iran’s ever more devastating economic crisis deepens, experts warn, Iranian leaders may feel they have little to lose by responding to U.S. pressure with the kind of military escalation President Trump now seems keen to avoid.

“The danger is that ‘economic D-Day’ is being presented almost as a substitute for further war when it may instead become another mechanism for escalating it,” said Sina Toossi, an Iran expert at the Center for International Policy. “The harder Washington pushes third countries to sever Iran’s remaining lifelines, the stronger Tehran’s incentive becomes to demonstrate that participating in Iran’s isolation carries costs of its own.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced a new package of U.S. measures to disrupt Iran’s economy, although he offered few details. The success of the U.S. efforts will also depend on how much the Trump administration can convince other countries to go along with its plan — especially critical trade partners for Iran, like Turkey, Russia, and China.

Still, as the Trump administration reached for military metaphors to convey the severity of its plans — calling them an “economic D-Day”— Iran responded in kind. Iranian officials have labeled the U.S. campaign the next phase of the war that Washington has waged since U.S.-Israeli strikes were launched in February.

Economic warfare is the “main battlefield” in the current confrontation, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corps was quoted as saying in a statement on Monday cited by Press TV, an Iranian state news outlet.

In statements broadcast after Mr. Bessent’s news conference, Iran’s economy minister, Ali Madanizadeh, warned that the country would find ways to push back.

“The enemies intend to launch an economic terrorist attack on us, but we also have our own tools and know how to play the game,” he said, in comments carried by the semiofficial news agency, Tasnim.

A day before Mr. Bessent’s announcements, Iran’s top security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, vowed that “not a single drop” of oil would leave the region if its Gulf neighbors joined the U.S. effort, and that they would be considered enemy states.

The severity of the Iranian warnings also highlights just how bad Iran’s current economic crisis is — and it is worsening by the day.

A report on Monday by Iran’s most prominent economic newspaper, Donya-e-Eghtesad, said Iran’s rial has depreciated to new lows. It has plummeted by 41 percent since December, when the currency rate sparked protests that morphed into weeks of nationwide unrest. Iranian security forces responded with a deadly crackdown.

Inflation and unemployment have soared, with prices of everyday goods increasingly out of reach for many Iranians. At the same time, the U.S. strikes that damaged Iranian energy infrastructure and the ongoing U.S. naval blockade have intensified an ever-worsening fuel supply crisis — an issue that sparked massive protests in 2019.

But Iranian officials are projecting confidence that their leadership can survive because this new wave of U.S. measures looks similar to old ones. For decades, American leaders have vowed to devastate the Iranian economy through ever harsher sanctions that the Islamic Republic’s leaders have learned to withstand.

Iran’s leadership “has been planning to confront U.S. sanctions for a long time and is fully prepared for new sanctions,” Mr. Madanizadeh, the economy minister, said late on Monday. He said the government had a two-year plan in place for dealing with such sanctions.

Iran’s ability to withstand the Trump administration’s economic pressure campaign will depend on the attitude of Iran’s key trading partners.

Mahdi Ghodsi, an economist at the Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies, said that “faced with sufficiently credible secondary-sanctions risks,” those trading partners may “prefer to protect their much more important financial and commercial interests with the United States and reduce the services they provide to Iranian entities.”

Some analysts also warn that the brunt of further economic pain is likely to be borne by ordinary Iranians, not Iran’s leaders.

Among the sectors Mr. Bessent identified as being targeted in the new U.S. campaign were gold, digital assets, technology, aviation and shipping — sectors that Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, who heads the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation, a London-based think tank focused on Iran’s economy, called “lifelines for the Iranian people.”

“Digital assets and gold are how ordinary Iranians protect their savings from inflation,” he wrote in a social media post. “Technology keeps Iranians connected with the world. Aviation keeps Iranian families connected with loved ones across borders. Shipping is how essential goods, including food and medicine, reach Iran.”

Sanam Mahoozi contributed reporting
